How does a leaf blower work?
The basic mechanics for a garden leaf blower are not all that different from the basic mechanics of a lawnmower. In lawnmowers, the main goal is to rotate blades in a controlled way to cut the grass. Leaf blowers work in a similar way, but with one big difference: Instead of rotating blades, you have a fan that shoots a blast of air. In addition, you have a motor that powers the fan.
Let's look in further detail at what a leaf blower is and how you can take care of it. How do blowers work?
The most typical leaf blowers today are corded leaf blowers, which are powered by electricity. With these blowers you connect a long extension cord between the leaf blower and the household electricity source. Cordless leaf blowers, on the other hand, do not use electricity and are powered by gas, similar to a lawnmower.
How are leaf blower rated?
In addition to power ratings and wattage, it is important to look at the engine, air filter and air speed to determine whether a leaf blower is adequate for your needs.
There is a minimum power rating for the blower, so take that into account based on the type of leaves you need to blow away, as well as the condition of your garden. You also have to find out how much air the blower can deliver and how smoothly it runs and how well it clears leaves.
Engine power for a leaf blower
Corded leaf blower
If you prefer a corded blower because you do not want to worry about refilling the tank, then a high engine power is important, especially as the amount of energy used by a blower is proportional to that of the electric motor.
The majority of blowers have two-stroke engines, meaning that gas and air enter the engine along with air that is mixed with fuel and ignited for combustion. This is the same process in the engine of a lawnmower.
Two stroke engines are much better than four stroke or diesel-fueled units. Not only do two-stroke engines have a higher energy and power consumption when operating, but they also require lower maintenance costs.
